blocks.content: Mentoring engineers covered a deliberate, longer horizon investment in one person growth. Influencing decisions widens the scope again, to shaping a genuine technical direction at the org level, across multiple teams, not just within your own immediate team where you may already have natural credibility and relationships.

This builds directly on the earlier influencing others topic from the communication skills module, but applied at a genuinely larger, more demanding scale, where the audience is not one person or one team, but multiple teams with genuinely different priorities and context.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784025580361-959341690.png
blocks.alt: Influencing decisions covers shaping a technical direction at the org level, across multiple teams, not just within your own team

blocks.content: 1. Influencing Within Your Team Versus Across the Org
blocks.text: 1. Influencing Within Your Team Versus Across the Org

blocks.content: Influencing within your own team benefits from shared context and existing relationships that already help, your teammates already know you, already share your team specific priorities, which makes earning buy in meaningfully easier.

Influencing at the org level, across many teams, involves genuinely less shared context and far more stakeholders to align, each with their own priorities, their own existing commitments, and often no prior working relationship with you at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784025582206-405566403.png
blocks.alt: Influencing within your own team benefits from shared context and existing relationships; influencing at the org level involves far less shared context and more stakeholders

blocks.content: 2. Why Org Level Influence Is Genuinely Harder
blocks.text: 2. Why Org Level Influence Is Genuinely Harder

blocks.content: A few real structural reasons make this genuinely harder than team level influence. There is no single audience, but many teams, each with different priorities and constraints, meaning a single message rarely resonates identically across all of them. Your direct authority typically covers only part of the org, meaning most of the actual influence has to be earned rather than simply exercised.

And the decisions being shaped affect people you may never interact with directly, which means the case being made has to hold up on its own merits, not just on personal relationship or trust built through direct interaction.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784025583965-106255953.png
blocks.alt: Org level influence is harder because there is no single audience, your direct authority covers only part of the org, and decisions affect people you may never meet

blocks.content: 3. A Worked Example

A concrete story shows this applied well. A recurring technical problem was noticed affecting multiple teams, not just the immediate team, suggesting a shared solution might be more valuable than an isolated, local fix.

First person quote: "I noticed a recurring technical problem affecting multiple teams, not just my own, which suggested it was worth solving at a broader level rather than patching it locally each time. I built real evidence from specific incidents across those different teams, rather than relying purely on my own team experience. I socialized the idea individually with key stakeholders from each affected team before making any wider proposal, so I understood their specific concerns first. The org ultimately adopted a shared standard that addressed the problem broadly, not just within my own team."
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784025585671-285962368.png
blocks.alt: A worked example: building cross team evidence, socializing the idea individually with key stakeholders first, and the org adopting a shared standard

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Making a wider proposal to the entire org before individually socializing the idea with key stakeholders first. A proposal that arrives without any prior context or relationship tends to face far more resistance than one that has already been discussed individually.
4. Building Genuine Support at the Org Level
blocks.text: 4. Building Genuine Support at the Org Level

blocks.content: A few concrete practices genuinely help at this scale. Grounding the case in real evidence spanning multiple teams, not just your own team specific experience, since org level decisions need org level evidence to be genuinely convincing. Talking to key stakeholders individually before a wider proposal, building understanding and early support one relationship at a time.

And honestly addressing the real, different priorities of other teams, rather than assuming your own team priorities automatically apply everywhere, since a proposal that ignores genuinely different priorities elsewhere in the org tends to face real, legitimate resistance.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784025587323-981821258.png
blocks.alt: Building org level support: ground the case in cross team evidence, socialize individually with key stakeholders first, and honestly address different team priorities

5. A Fix Scoped to One Team Versus a Broad Standard
blocks.text: 5. A Fix Scoped to One Team Versus a Broad Standard

blocks.content: A fix scoped only to your own team solves the problem locally, which is genuinely valuable, but leaves every other team facing the same underlying issue to solve it independently, often less efficiently, or not at all.

A shared standard adopted more broadly solves the problem for many teams at once, which requires meaningfully more work to actually build genuine org wide support, but produces a far larger total impact than any single team local fix ever could.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784025588956-180735661.png
blocks.alt: A fix scoped to one team solves it locally but leaves other teams facing the same issue; a shared standard adopted broadly solves it for many teams at once

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: The extra effort required to build genuine org level support is usually worth it specifically when the underlying problem genuinely affects multiple teams, not just your own.
6. Genuinely Common Failure Modes

A few real patterns undermine influencing decisions at the org level. Proposing broadly before building any individual stakeholder support first, which tends to face far more resistance than a proposal introduced with prior context. Ignoring the real, different priorities of other teams, treating your own team perspective as if it automatically applied everywhere.

And relying purely on personal authority or seniority rather than genuine evidence, which tends not to hold up well once the proposal reaches teams where you have no direct relationship or existing credibility.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784025590527-252041052.png
blocks.alt: Common failure modes: proposing broadly with no individual groundwork, ignoring different team priorities, and relying on authority instead of genuine evidence

blocks.content: 7. Choosing Your Own Influencing Decisions Story
blocks.text: 7. Choosing Your Own Influencing Decisions Story

blocks.content: Look for a real situation where you genuinely shaped a technical direction affecting multiple teams, not just your own, and where you can describe the specific evidence gathered and the individual relationship building that made broader adoption possible.

The strongest stories here show real evidence spanning multiple teams and individual groundwork done before any wider proposal, since both together are usually what separates genuine org level influence from a proposal that simply happened to get lucky.
Influence at the org level is built one honest conversation at a time, before it is ever proposed to everyone at once.
